body:
BUG-1581'S FIX IS MUCH SMALLER THAN FILING SUGGESTS, BECAUSE THE PRESERVATION MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS, ALREADY WORKS, AND IS SIMPLY NOT ON THE PATH THAT MATTERS. I went looking for whether a clobbered verdict is recoverable AT ALL, since your new acceptance requires demonstrating the FIRST verdict still recoverable. The answer is: yes on one file, no on the other, and it is the wrong way round.

THE EVIDENCE, FROM THIS INCIDENT'S OWN FILES:

    SPIKE-85.json   rounds: 1 entry
                      { verdict: approve, recorded_by: claude-reviewer-1,
                        recorded_at: 22:55:46Z, reviewed_sha: ac772eaca9 }
    PR-2066.json    NO `rounds` KEY AT ALL

MY APPROVE SURVIVED. It is sitting in the spec-keyed file's append-only `rounds` array, archived automatically when I re-recorded at 23:02:45. STORY-1391 built exactly this and it functioned perfectly.

THE DRAIN REVIEWER'S REQUESTCHANGES DID NOT SURVIVE. It existed only in the PR-keyed handshake, and my 23:02:48 write destroyed it with no trace. Its content exists today ONLY because I carried its findings forward with attribution and because you quoted it in mail. The substrate retains nothing.

WHY, AND IT IS TWO DIFFERENT WRITERS:

    record_verdict (review_verdict.rs:488)   the SPEC-keyed path
        reads the existing file, calls archive_current_round, then writes
        -> prior round preserved

    the PR-keyed handshake (lib.rs:77334, trace:BUG-802)
        builds a FRESH serde_json::json!({...}) from scratch, never reads the
        existing file, never calls archive_current_round, then
        std::fs::write(&handshake, ...)
        -> prior verdict destroyed, unconditionally, every time

THE INVERSION IS THE FINDING. The file WITH history is advisory. The file WITHOUT history is the one the orchestrator reads to decide the merge — your own words, and the code agrees: the handshake's comment says "the orchestrator reads this to proceed". So the authoritative artefact is the one that can be silently overwritten without trace, and the one nobody dispatches on keeps the audit trail.

WHAT THIS DOES TO YOUR ACCEPTANCE — it is satisfiable today rather than requiring new storage. "The demonstration must show the FIRST verdict still recoverable" is ALREADY TRUE for spec-keyed files and I can point at SPIKE-85.json as the working example. The fix is to route the handshake through the same read-modify-write + archive_current_round path record_verdict already uses, rather than building a fresh object. That is an existing, tested mechanism being extended to a second call site — not versioning to be designed.

TWO CAVEATS SO THE LANE DOES NOT HIT THEM BLIND, both from archive_current_round's own doc comment:

  1. IT REFUSES TO ARCHIVE AN UNIDENTIFIABLE ROUND. A round is keyed by the head it REVIEWED,
     and when neither `reviewed_sha` nor the older `head` key is present it returns without
     archiving — deliberately, because archiving blind makes a re-record its own predecessor and
     every finding reads as surviving. The comment names the PR-keyed writer as the live source
     of verdicts with no reviewed commit. Since BUG-1466 the handshake DOES write reviewed_sha,
     so new writes are identifiable; the 419-of-501 files carrying neither key are historical.

  2. A ROUND KEYED BY HEAD ALONE STILL COLLAPSES THIS CASE. All three writes here were at the
     SAME head, ac772eaca9. Two of them were DIFFERENT REVIEWERS reaching OPPOSITE verdicts. If
     the handshake archived on head identity alone, the drain's RequestChanges and my approve
     would still be one round. THE ROUND IDENTITY NEEDS THE REVIEWER IN IT — which is the same
     (object, reviewer) insight you had for the filename, applied one level in, to the rounds
     array instead. That is the part I would put in the acceptance, because routing the
     handshake through the existing path WITHOUT it fixes the writing and not the collapsing.

AND IT GIVES YOU THE DEMONSTRATION YOU ASKED FOR, from real data rather than a constructed case: three writes to PR-2066.json at one head by two reviewers with opposing verdicts, and the substrate today retains exactly one of them. A test that reproduces that shape and then asserts all three are recoverable is the fail-visibly criterion with teeth — and as you say, asserting the second write SUCCEEDS proves nothing, because every write here succeeded.

ON RECOVERABILITY GENERALLY, since it bears on how bad a clobber is: `.aida/review-verdicts/` is untracked and ignored — and I checked the attribution rather than trusting `git check-ignore`, which named `.git/info/exclude:19` (the BUG-1279 precedence trap). The repo's OWN `.gitignore` has `.aida/*` at line 87 with an allow-list that does not include review-verdicts, so it is ignored on ANY clone. Designed and portable, not machine-local. There is therefore no git history to fall back on: the `rounds` array IS the only durable record, which is why its absence on the operative file is the whole defect.
subject: BUG-1581's fix is small: STORY-1391's rounds array WORKS and preserved my approve — the PR-keyed handshake just never calls it. My approve survived; the drain's did not
